value.overview: The Jabiru (Jabiru mycteria), also called the Jabiru Stork, is one of the largest flying birds in the Americas and the tallest stork in the New World. It lives mainly in lowland wetlands, where its long legs and massive bill help it forage in shallow water. Adults are mostly white with a black head and neck marked by a red throat pouch. In Costa Rica, it is a scarce and locally important wetland bird.
value.classification: The Jabiru belongs to the stork family Ciconiidae and is the only species in the genus Jabiru. It is not closely related to the smaller Wood Stork, despite sharing wetland habitats.
value.identification: This very large stork stands about 1.2–1.4 meters tall and has a broad wingspan. Adults have white plumage, black bare skin on the head and upper neck, and a conspicuous red pouch at the base of the neck. The heavy, slightly upturned bill is black. In flight, the bird shows broad wings, a long neck, and long legs extending beyond the tail. Young birds are duller and lack the strongly developed red throat pouch.
value.rangeHabitat: The Jabiru ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and much of tropical South America, mainly east of the Andes. In Costa Rica it is highly localized, occurring chiefly in the lower Tempisque basin and northern lowlands around Caño Negro, Medio Queso, Upala, and nearby wetlands. It uses freshwater marshes, seasonal lagoons, flooded savannas, shallow ponds, drainage channels, rice fields, and other open wetlands. Nesting commonly occurs in tall trees standing in or near seasonally flooded woodland.
value.migrationStatus: The Jabiru is generally resident or locally dispersive rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it occurs year-round in suitable wetland regions, but numbers and records may increase seasonally, especially from roughly November to March, when water conditions and food availability change. Individuals can move between the Tempisque wetlands and northern Caribbean-slope lowlands.
value.breeding: Jabirus form large stick nests high in mature trees, often in floodplain or wetland woodland. Nest trees reported in Costa Rica include white guanacaste, kapok, rosewood-related species, and other large native trees. The nest may be very broad and is usually placed well above the ground on strong branches. Both adults participate in nest construction and care for the young. Breeding success depends on retaining suitable nesting trees, nearby shallow feeding areas, and quiet conditions around active nests.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of fish, including swamp eels and other small wetland fish, but also includes frogs, small reptiles, aquatic invertebrates, crustaceans, and occasionally other small animals. Jabirus usually walk slowly through shallow water or soft mud, probing and snapping with the bill. In Costa Rica they forage in marshes, lagoons, canals, and flooded agricultural fields, sometimes alone and sometimes among other waterbirds.
value.behavior: Jabirus are usually quiet, deliberate birds that spend much of the day walking through wetlands or resting in tall trees. They may soar on broad wings during local movements and often gather where prey is concentrated. Courtship and social displays can include raised wings, bill movements, and postural displays. Despite their size, they are capable fliers. They are sensitive to disturbance near nests and may leave protected wetlands temporarily to feed in nearby farmland or artificial water bodies.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not considered strongly stable across the entire range, and declines or continuing range reductions have been reported in some areas. In Costa Rica, the population is small and has declined markedly from historical levels; published national estimates have generally placed the remaining population at fewer than 100 individuals, although the exact current number is uncertain.
conservation.threats: Important threats in Costa Rica include the loss and alteration of freshwater wetlands, drainage and conversion of marshes, contamination by pesticides and other pollutants, disturbance at nesting sites, and the removal of large mature trees used for nesting. Dependence on shallow wetlands and specific nesting trees makes the national population especially vulnerable. Feeding in agricultural landscapes can also expose birds to contaminated water and human disturbance.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore the lower Tempisque, Caño Negro, Medio Queso, and other northern lowland wetlands. Retain large native trees near marshes and safeguard active nests with an adequate disturbance buffer. Reduce pesticide and fertilizer runoff, maintain shallow-water feeding areas, and support wetland monitoring and local conservation programs. Visitors should observe Jabirus from a distance, avoid approaching nests, and report sightings through reputable bird-monitoring projects.
